-2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ c\\end{aligned}].\n$$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form\n\n$$\nx=Au+b,\n$$\n\nwhere $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nReversing the action of $T,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\\\ Au & =x-b \\\\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:\n\n$$\n{{[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & 2\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\\cdot {{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\n$$\n\nNext, we calculate the inverse of $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{2\\cdot 2-1\\cdot 5}[\\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\\\ -5 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{-1}[\\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\\\ -5 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & -2\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\\cdot ({{[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & -2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]-[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & -2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & -2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]-[\\begin{aligned}-3 \\\\ 8\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\\\ 5 & -2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ -8\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\na+b+c=-2+1+(-8)=-9.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186180005 :question/id #uuid form\n\n$$\nx=Au+b,\n$$\n\nwhere $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nReversing the action of $T,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\\\ Au & =x-b \\\\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2u-3v+2 \\\\ 6v-3u-4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\\\ -3u+6v\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & ={{[\\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\\\ -3 & 6\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\\cdot {{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we calculate the inverse of $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{6\\cdot 2-(-3)\\cdot (-3)}[\\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\\\ 3 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\\\ 3 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\\cdot ({{[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x-2 \\\\ y+4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2\\cdot (x-2)+1\\cdot (y+4) \\\\ 1\\cdot (x-2)+(\\frac{2}{3})\\cdot (y+4)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2x+y \\\\ x+\\frac{2}{3}y+\\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEquating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is\n\n$$\nu=2x+y+0,\\,v=x+\\frac{2}{3}y+\\frac{2}{3}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\na+b+c=0+\\frac{2}{3}+\\frac{2}{3}=\\frac{4}{3}.\n$$"} "![](images/3f/3f8c1c9854ec54dd3caf4487328d3f3c35f2d69680a8fd1c13d28125dac77d03.png)\n\nConsider the affine transformation $T,$ given by\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 \\\\ 1 & -3\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n \nWhat would be the image of the square shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any affine transformation \n\n$$\nT:u⟶Au+b,\n$$\n\nwhere $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:\n\n- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.\n\n- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:\n\n- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.\n\n- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our transformation.\n\nNotice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is \n$A=[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 \\\\ 1 & -3\\end{aligned}].$\n\nComputing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\\begin{aligned}-2 & 6 \\\\ 1 & -3\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot (-3)-6\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have a singular nonzero matrix. \n\nTherefore, $T$ is non-invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} {:db/id 17592186180090 3\\end{aligned}]}_{\\mathbf b}.$$\n\nWe wish to determine whether $\\mathbf T^{-1}$ exists and find its matrix form if it does exist.\n\nComputing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\\det(A) = \\left| \\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\\\ 1 & -2\\end{aligned} \\right| = 1\\cdot (-2) - (-3) \\cdot 1 = 1 \\neq 0.$$\n\nSince $\\det(A) \\neq 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible.\n\nTo compute the inverse y\\end{aligned}]-[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\\\ -1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\ & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\\\ -1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]-[\\begin{aligned}5 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\ & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\\\ -1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}-5 \\\\ "35abe35f-9e29-539b-aaa5-a2546fd2fbfb" :step/math-academy-id 44704} {:db/id 17592186180569 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180761 :tutorial/content "Consider the square in the $uv$-plane shown below.\n\n![](images/a8/a8cc0923da86a1a1ac6b666893397263ef3865448080500caa6f17510547d901.png)\n\nWe wish to explore the image of this square under an affine transformation $$\\mathbf{T}: \\mathbf{u} \\longrightarrow A \\mathbf{u} + \\mathbf{b},$$ where $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix, and $\\mathbf u$ and $\\mathbf b$ are $2\\times 1$ column vectors.\n\nSimilar to linear transformations, there are three possibilities depending on the value of $\\det(A)$.\n\n- $\\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular ($\\det(A)\\neq 0$). In this case, our square is mapped to a parallelogram.\n\nFor example, let the transformation $\\mathbf T$ be given by $$[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] = [\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\cdot [\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}] + [\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane, we get the following parallelogram:\n\n![](images/36/36da067393fa53f4296373d65e3c6177a54d1a901824188687b4a74ea171afdf.png)\n- $\\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\\det(A)=0$) and $A$ has at least one nonzero entry. In this case, our square is mapped to a line segment.\n\nFor example, let the transformation $\\mathbf T$ be given by $$[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] = [\\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\\\ 2 & -1\\end{aligned}] \\cdot [\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}] + [\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following line segment:\n\n![](images/5e/5e5481e5b2f2218a6097020e260dc991cde05574372c724aa07527458257d94c.png)\n- $\\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\\det(A)=0$) and $A$ is the zero matrix. In this case, our square is mapped to a point on the plane.\n\nFor example, let the transformation $\\mathbf T$ be given by $$[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] = [\\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0\\end{aligned}] \\cdot [\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}] + [\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following point.\n\n![](images/00/0072c5e06674f79f82e771744fda217e6558830f7a6e4ab387aa9dbf4dda09bc.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "375d6591-08dd-5dbf-b36a-28013839a28b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7706 :tutorial/title "Image Types Formed by Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "5ec4662b-6870-532f-83f9-f7a9cbe5504e" :step/math-academy-id 44705 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180570}} {:db/id 17592186180570 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180762 :tutorial/content "In general, if we consider the affine transformation $\\mathbf T:\\Bbb R^2 \\to \\Bbb R^2,$ defined by the mapping\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{T}: \\mathbf{u} \\longrightarrow A \\mathbf{u} + \\mathbf{b},\n$$\n\nwhere $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix and $\\mathbf u$ and $\\mathbf b$ are $2\\times 1$ column vectors, then we have one of the following three possibilities:\n\n- If $\\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\\det(A) \\neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.\n\n- If $\\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases: \n\n- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.\n\n- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane (namely, the point with position vector $\\mathbf b$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "560907bc-354a-5693-a8df-e6824454755d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7710 :tutorial/title "A Summary of Image Types"} :step/id #uuid "d71cf118-7383-5aea-a47c-8359fc7dffe4" :step/math-academy-id 44723 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180568}}] :activity/title "The Inverse of an Affine Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179860} {:db/id 17592186180559 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180757 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\\mathbf T:\\mathbb R^2\\rightarrow\\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. Additionally, we have the following:\n\n*An affine transformation $\\mathbf T$ is invertible if and only if the matrix $A$ that represents the linear transformation associated with $\\mathbf T$ is invertible, that is, $\\det(A) \\neq 0.$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "bf99caa7-1e47-5fea-87ac-9b91151af127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7697 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180560 :step/content :question/math-academy-id "q-124289" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as\n\n$$\nx=u-v-1,\\,y=3v-2u-6.\n$$\n\nGiven that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is\n\n$$\nu=ax+y+9,\\,v=bx+y+c,\n$$\n\nwhat is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form\n\n$$\nx=Au+b,\n$$\n\nwhere $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nReversing the action of $T,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\\\ Au & =x-b \\\\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}u-v-1 \\\\ 3v-2u-6\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}u-v \\\\ -2u+3v\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ -6\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & ={{[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\\\ -2 & 3\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\\cdot {{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ -6\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we calculate the inverse of $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{3\\cdot 1-(-1)\\cdot (-2)}[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\\cdot ({{[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ -6\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x+1 \\\\ y+6\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3\\cdot (x+1)+1\\cdot (y+6) \\\\ 2\\cdot (x+1)+1\\cdot (y+6)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3x+y+9 \\\\ 2x+y+8\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEquating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is\n\n$$\nu=3x+y+9,\\,v=2x+y+8.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\na+b+c=3+2+8=13.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7332e33-ee2f-5908-9f85-c258b5d80b5d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406972}} {:db/id 17592186406974 :step/content {:db/id 17592186259649 affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form\n\n$$\nx=Au+b,\n$$\n\nwhere $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nReversing the action of $T,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\\\ Au & =x-b \\\\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2-u-v \\\\ 3u+4v-1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-u-v \\\\ 3u+4v\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & ={{[\\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\\\ 3 & 4\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\\cdot {{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we calculate the inverse of $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{4\\cdot (-1)-(-1)\\cdot 3}[\\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\\\ -3 & -1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{-1}[\\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\\\ -3 & -1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\\\ 3 & 1\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\\\ 3 & 1\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\\cdot ({{[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\\\ 3 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x-2 \\\\ y+1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-4\\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\\cdot (y+1) \\\\ 3\\cdot (x-2)+1\\cdot (y+1)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}7-4x-y \\\\ 3x+y-5\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEquating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is\n\n$$\nu=7+(-4)x-y,\\,v=3x+y+(-5).\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\na+b+c=-4+3+(-5)=-6.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "c564b67d-ab6c-5a8c-9962-63cefc9e226d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406973}} {:db/id 17592186406971 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406968 nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.\n\n- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.\n\nWith #uuid "6d452c80-d748-5af8-bbed-4f41e3a6ab8b" :question/math-academy-id "q-124314" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as\n\n$$\nx=2u-3v+2,\\,y=6v-3u-4.\n$$\n\nGiven that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is\n\n$$\nu=2x+y+a,\\,v=x+by+c,\n$$\n\nwhat is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form\n\n$$\nx=Au+b,\n$$\n\nwhere $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nReversing the action of $T,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\\\ Au & =x-b \\\\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2u-3v+2 \\\\ 6v-3u-4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\\\ -3u+6v\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & ={{[\\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\\\ -3 & 6\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\\cdot {{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we calculate the inverse of $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{6\\cdot 2-(-3)\\cdot (-3)}[\\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\\\ 3 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\\\ 3 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\\cdot ({{[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}x-2 \\\\ y+4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2\\cdot (x-2)+1\\cdot (y+4) \\\\ 1\\cdot (x-2)+(\\frac{2}{3})\\cdot (y+4)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2x+y \\\\ x+\\frac{2}{3}y+\\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nEquating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is\n\n$$\nu=2x+y+0,\\,v=x+\\frac{2}{3}y+\\frac{2}{3}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\na+b+c=0+\\frac{2}{3}+\\frac{2}{3}=\\frac{4}{3}.\n$$"} $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nReversing the action of $T,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\\\ Au & =x-b \\\\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2u-3v+2 \\\\ 6v-3u-4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\\\ -3u+6v\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & ={{[\\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\\\ -3 & & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{{[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\\cdot ({{[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1005 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
